 Judgment
Though matter is listed for arguments on admission, with the consent of learned counsel for parties it is taken up for final disposal.
2. This appeal is filed by the petitioner seeking enhancement of compensation awarded by the tribunal.
3. The parties are referred to as per the rankings before the tribunal.
4. Learned counsel for the appellant has submitted his arguments that quantum of the compensation determined by the tribunal is quite on the lower side and same is liable to be enhanced.
Further it is submitted that vehicle involved in the accident is insured with respondent No.2-insurance company and the policy was in force as on the date of accident.
However, tribunal has not considered the same and dismissed the claim petition against the insurance company.
On all these grounds sought for allowing the appeal.
5. As against this, learned counsel for the respondent - insurance company has submitted his arguments that tribunal has passed the impugned judgment and award in accordance with law and facts.
That there are no grounds to interfere with the impugned judgment and award and sought for dismissal of this appeal.

To substantiate her arguments she relied on the decision of Coordinate Bench of this Court in the case of NATIONAL INSURANCE CO. LTD., HAVERI v.
RUDREGOWDA @ RUDREGOWDAPPA SHIVANNAGOWDA AND ANOTHER reported in (2012)
KARN MAC 456 (KANT).
6.

7. My answer to above points are:
(1) Partly affirmative.

sentences.text: With regard to the notional income of the injured is concerned, the Tribunal has assessed the income of the injured at Rs.4,000/- per month.
In view of the guidelines issued by the Karnataka State Legal Services Authority, a sum of Rs.6,500/- has to be taken into consideration as notional income.
Then it comes to Rs.6,500/- x 12 x 18 x 10% = Rs.1,40,400/-, which is rounded off to Rs.1,40,000/-.
Accordingly the petitioner is entitled for compensation of Rs.1,40,000/- towards loss of future income.

RE. POINT NO.2:
11.

With regard to liability of the insurance company is concerned, in para 21 and 22 of the impugned judgment the tribunal has observed as under:
"21.
The Ex.R1 is the "Act policy" of insurance issued by the respondent No.2/insurance Company to the vehicle of respondent No.1.
In the light of this evidence, Sri. K.H.P. Advocate relying upon the ruling reported in 2012 Karn.
MAC 456 between National Insurance Co., Ltd., vs. Rudregouda, argued that the Ex.RI covers the risk to the petitioner as he was proceeding alongwith the goods.

sentences.text: I have gone through the entire discussion made by the Hon'ble High Court.
The vehicle involved before the Hon'ble High Court was a heavy goods vehicle, i.e. lorry having 5 +1 capacity of seating in the cabin as per rule 100 of the M.V.Act.

In the present case,
Appe auto admittedly goods vehicle having only one seating capacity that too for driver only.

Even petitioner himself produced RC of the said auto as per Ex.P41, the Pradeep S/O Ashok Mahindrakar vs Hyder S/O Maheboob Ali on 19 April, 2023 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/35996337/
3 same clearly revealing the seating capacity is only one.

entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: Admittedly there is no any seating arrangement on the backside of the vehicle.
Muchless, there is no iota of evidence what kind of tent materials was carrying on the day of accident.
Since the auto was a light motor vehicle seating capacity is only one and except driver and goods, it is not permitted to carry any other person.

However, goods was carrying alongwith four persons as disclosed from the own evidence of P.w-1.
22.
Looking to the Ex R-1, there is no extra premium covering risk the to any of passenger other than the driver as permitted in the RC.

Thus, having regard to the nature of policy of insurance coupled with seating capacity of the vehicle, it is my considered opinion that though the petitioner considered as proceeding alongwith goods, the risk is not covered in the" Act policy of insurance".
To the present facts of the case and nature of the vehicle, the ruling relied upon by the counsel for the petitioner is not applicable.
Admittedly, in the present case Pw-I was not in the cabin.
The Ape auto is a private goods vehicle and under the Act policy the occupants of the same are not covered as per the dictum laid down by the Hon'ble Apex court in AIR 2008 SC 2729.
So far as the another contention of the insurance company about non holding of driving licence to the auto driver, no cogent evidence is placed.
Per contra, the petitioner produced the driving license.
Accordingly.
I am of the view that the insurance company failed to prove its contention of non- holding of the driving license by its insured driver.

However, it is successfully established that the insurance company not liable to pay the compensation on the ground that the petitioner was an unauthorised passenger in the goods auto and thereupon the respondent No.1 violated the policy terms and conditions.

With these observations, I am of the view that the respondent No.1 being the owner of the Appe auto alone is held responsible to pay compensation to the petitioner to the tune of Rs.2,02,700/- with interest at the rate of 6% p.a. from the date of petition till its realisation.
Accordingly, my finding on issue No.3 is in the negative and issue No.4 is in the affirmative against respondent No.1 alone."
12. This Court has reappreciated the evidence on record.
On perusal of FIR-Ex.P-1 and complaint - Ex.P-2 it is crystal clear that the petitioner was travelling in goods vehicle - Appe Auto by carrying the goods.
Spot mahazar also reveals the same.
Ex.P-44 - charge sheet also discloses the same.
To substantiate this documentary evidence the petitioner is examined as PW1.
He has deposed as to the averments made in the FIR, complaint and also charge sheet.

During the course of cross examination of RW1-S.V.Bhaskar, S/o.Sadanand, Administrative Officer of National Insurance Co.
Ltd., has clearly admitted in his evidence that petitioner was travelling in a goods vehicle along with the goods.
13. Though appellant was travelling in the goods vehicle along with goods, the Tribunal has not considered the same and tribunal has observed that petitioner was travelling in a vehicle as an unauthorised passenger, which is contrary to the fact.

The tribunal has not properly appreciated the Pradeep S/O Ashok Mahindrakar vs Hyder S/O Maheboob Ali on 19 April, 2023 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/35996337/
4 evidence on record in accordance with law and facts.

sentences.text: The tribunal has ignored the oral and documentary evidence placed by both the parties.
Even the Tribunal has ignored the admissions made by the RW1, which cannot be accepted.

14. In Ex.R-1-policy of the insurance reveals that policy covers use only under a permit within the meaning of the Motor Vehicle Act, 1988 or such a carriage falling under sub-section 3 of Section 66 of the Motor Vehicles Act, 1988.
The policy does not cover use for (a) Organised racing (b) Pace Making (c) Reliability Trials (d) Speed Testing 15.

In the case on hand, the IO has not submitted the charge sheet against the driver of the vehicle for the commission of offences punishable under Section 66 r/w Section 192A of Motor Vehicles Act,
1988.
16.
The respondent-insurance company has not placed any materials to show that appellant was travelling in a goods vehicle as unauthorised passenger.
Therefore, considering the facts and circumstances of the case, I am of the considered view that insurance company is liable to - 10 - pay the compensation.
Hence, I answer Point No.2 in partly affirmative.

ORDER (a) The appeal is allowed in part.

(b) The judgment and award dated  18.02.2015 passed by the Additional Senior Civil Judge & CJM & Addl. MACT, Bidar, in MVC No.319/2013, in respect of dismissal of the claim petition against respondent No.2 - insurance company is set aside.
